entries.title: ChainDrop: Self-propagating npm worm mints valid Sigstore provenance and exfiltrates via Ethereum-routed C2
entries.summary: Unit 42 analyzed a self-propagating npm worm that infected 400+ packages (collectively hundreds of millions of weekly downloads). Once a stolen npm token or a repo-scoped OIDC exchange gives the worm publish rights, it mints a real Sigstore in-toto SLSA v1 provenance attestation for the infected tarball — so signature-checking pipelines see valid provenance for malicious code. C2 domains resolve through an Ethereum smart contract, letting the operator rotate infrastructure with one on-chain transaction and no malware update.
entries.takeaway: Valid npm provenance no longer distinguishes a safe artifact from an evasive one — pivot on the Rekor log identity and workflow, not on signature-checks-pass.

lessons.point: Valid Sigstore provenance is not evidence a package is clean — a worm can mint real attestations against its own compromised workflow.
lessons.excerpt: Given the reality of today's npm supply chain threats, a package having valid npm provenance does not mean the package is clean. It only means the tarball came out of the workflow named in the certificate. If that workflow is running attacker code, valid provenance is what you should expect to see.

lessons.point: CI runner memory is a live credential target — the worm scrapes /proc/<pid>/mem on GitHub Actions Runner.Worker to capture OIDC tokens and runner secrets that would otherwise never touch disk.
lessons.excerpt: An embedded Python helper hidden inside an encrypted blob in the payload locates the Runner.Worker process on GitHub Actions runners, opens /proc/<pid>/maps and /proc/<pid>/mem, and searches live process memory for OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens and runner secrets.

lessons.point: AI-coding-tool configs (.claude/settings.json SessionStart hook, .vscode/tasks.json) are execution infrastructure — the worm writes cross-linked persistence into both directories.
lessons.excerpt: It writes a .vscode/tasks.json file with a task labeled Environment Setup and sets it to run when the folder opens... It also writes a .claude/settings.json file with a SessionStart command hook, meaning it executes whenever Claude Code starts a session in the project.

lessons.point: C2 domain resolution via a blockchain smart contract lets the operator silently reconfigure infrastructure with a single Ethereum transaction, without pushing any malware update.
lessons.excerpt: This C2 rotation demonstrates the adversary's ability to silently reconfigure the worm's entire C2 infrastructure through a single Ethereum transaction, without requiring any update to the deployed malware.

entries.threat: Worm-driven npm package compromise that steals cloud/CI/AI-tool credentials, chains publishing rights via OIDC trusted-publishing to mint valid provenance on infected packages, and persists inside developer environments through AI-coding-tool configuration files.
entries.conditions: npm-published package with preinstall hook AND developer or CI environment that runs 'npm install' or the equivalent; the worm auto-propagates once it captures an npm publishing token.
entries.mitigations: Grep for the 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again' marker in repo descriptions; hunt for .claude/settings.json + .vscode/tasks.json cross-linked droppers; treat valid npm provenance as authenticity, not integrity; monitor the Rekor transparency log for unexpected workflow identities; block both npm-cache[.]com and awqhnjewqjkl[.]icu; consider CI runners as credential-exfil targets and pin/audit dependencies rather than relying on provenance alone.
entries.prior_art: Continues the Shai-Hulud npm supply-chain lineage (JFrog, May 2026). Novel elements: Sigstore provenance mint via trusted-publishing OIDC, Ethereum-based C2 resolution, .claude/settings.json persistence, CI runner memory scraping.

actionable.title: Treat valid npm provenance as authenticity of source, not integrity of code
actionable.detail: Update your supply-chain gates: if you were relying on 'signature valid + provenance attests' as sufficient for trust, add a check that the workflow identity in the Rekor log matches an expected repo/workflow. Grep repos for .claude/settings.json + .vscode/tasks.json cross-linked droppers as a hunting signal.

entries.title: CRLF-Powered Desync Attacks: header injection escalates to CDN-wide response queue poisoning + browser-side XSS
entries.summary: Portswigger extend HTTP header injection into a full-blown desync worm and show novel browser-side techniques for connection-locked and IP-locked desyncs. In an nginx misconfiguration where $uri is included in proxy_pass, URL-encoded CRLF sequences in the request path are decoded before forwarding, giving an attacker complete control over the upstream request. Applied inside a CDN's infrastructure, this captured session cookies and auth tokens from thousands of unrelated applications.
entries.takeaway: HTTP header injection is severely underestimated — one nginx $uri-in-proxy_pass misconfig can escalate to CDN-wide response queue poisoning that harvests session cookies from unrelated tenants.

lessons.point: nginx URL-decodes the request path when $uri is used in proxy_pass, allowing encoded CRLF (%0d%0a) sequences to inject arbitrary headers into the upstream request.
lessons.excerpt: In Nginx configurations (an extremely popular web server) if the $uri variable is included in the proxy_pass directive, Nginx will normalise the request path before use, url-decoding any encoded characters including CRLF sequences (%0d%0a). This allows us to inject new lines into the request that is forwarded upstream of Nginx, giving us full control over the structure of that request.

lessons.point: Response Queue Poisoning inside a CDN's own infrastructure lets an attacker route requests to arbitrary tenant domains on that CDN — capturing session cookies and auth tokens across thousands of unrelated applications.
lessons.excerpt: Impact wise, as a result of capturing requests, we also started to capture session cookies and auth tokens for thousands of applications hosted on the CDN.

lessons.point: Request splitting with exactly two smuggled requests achieves RQP without any RFC violation — two CRLFs in a row are just another request boundary, so request splitting works out-of-the-box against many stacks.
lessons.excerpt: This technique does not breach the RFC using mutated headers in any way. Two CRLF sequences in a row, are simply another boundary between requests and as a result, this technique works exceptionally well out-of-the-box.

entries.threat: HTTP header injection in nginx (or any proxy) that normalises URL-decoded CRLF before upstream forwarding, escalated to Response Queue Poisoning inside CDNs to harvest cross-tenant sessions.
entries.conditions: Reverse proxy (typically nginx) with $uri or equivalent user-controlled path variable interpolated into proxy_pass without CRLF sanitisation.
entries.mitigations: Audit nginx configs for $uri-in-proxy_pass patterns; reject CRLF in decoded request paths at the proxy; deploy request-smuggling detection (Burp scan / dedicated proxy fuzzing) against CDN edges before assuming them safe.
entries.prior_art: Extends James Kettle's 'Making HTTP Header Injection Critical via RQP' (2023) and Sergey Bobrov's nginx misconfig research. This paper is the BHUSA/DEFCON 2026 followup that operationalizes the technique across CDN infrastructure and introduces browser-powered variants.

actionable.title: Audit nginx configs for $uri-in-proxy_pass
actionable.detail: grep -rn 'proxy_pass.*\$uri' /etc/nginx to find configs where CRLF injection is trivial. Also add request-smuggling scanning to CDN edge tests, not just app tests.

entries.title: Can AI do novel security research? Meet the HTTP Terminator
entries.summary: James Kettle built HTTP Terminator, an autonomous research pipeline that took 138 HTTP/SMTP RFCs, generated 15,000 micro-inspiration fragments and 30,000 candidate desync vectors, and evaluated them at 2,000-thread scale against 30,000 live bug-bounty targets — producing several novel desync triggers, a novel desync pattern (dual-matching Content-Length), a novel weaponization technique (dangling-byte for RQP), a novel attack concept (Shared-Parser Confusion), and CVE-2026-63078 in Apache Traffic Server. The transferable architecture is Ideation → Evaluation → Weaponization → Cascade with the design principle 'AI vs Code vs Human' — start LLM-heavy, migrate correctness-critical steps to deterministic code, keep the researcher in the discovery cascade.
entries.takeaway: Autonomous research works when you (a) design the evaluation primitive first, (b) migrate everything correctness-critical from LLM to code, and (c) put the human back in for the discovery cascade — not for individual verdicts.

lessons.point: System-design axis is not 'human vs AI' but AI vs Code vs Human: start LLM-heavy for speed, then migrate correctness-critical steps to deterministic code as the pipeline matures.
lessons.excerpt: It's better to frame system design as AI vs Code vs Human. You can start quickly with an AI-heavy approach, then gradually move responsibility to deterministic code to improve accuracy & speed.

lessons.point: Micro-inspiration beats broad prompting: splitting RFCs into 1-3 sentence fragments and asking for 1-5 vectors per fragment produced 30,000 unique triggers where naive prompting produced mostly retreads of Kettle's own prior work.
lessons.excerpt: The solution was micro-inspiration. I adapted the classic researcher strategy of reading RFCs for inspiration, and split the inputs into tiny fragments of 1-3 sentences each to solve the context-contamination problem and maximize the number of unique vectors generated.

lessons.point: Frontier models exhibit novice-pentester failure modes on specialist tasks — the elicitation gap is real and prompting alone doesn't close it; deterministic guardrails around agent output do.
lessons.excerpt: Even the most powerful frontier models replicated mistakes usually made by under-trained novice pentesters, such as seeing HTTP pipelining and thinking it shows a vulnerability

lessons.point: The most valuable discovery — Shared-Parser Confusion — was AI-proposed and human-validated, not fully autonomous. Autonomous cascades work; the human belongs specifically at the cascade step where a partial finding generalizes into an attack class.
lessons.excerpt: servers are using shared code to parse both requests and responses, so the attack-surface you can hit isn't limited to request features. That, by itself, is absolutely huge.

lessons.point: Reality-reframing the MCP tool interface (renaming Turbo Intruder to 'Turbo Simulator', hiding Connection: close headers, offering placebo connection-reuse) bypassed refusals and misinterpreted signals — controlling the agent's tool surface is a stronger lever than prompting.
lessons.excerpt: Since we control both the agent's prompt and the MCP interface it uses to interact with the real world, we effectively control its eyes, ears, and hands - its entire reality.

actionable.title: Autonomous security research loop: Ideation → Evaluation → Weaponization → Cascade
actionable.detail: Build research agents on Kettle's blueprint: (1) design the evaluation primitive first because it dictates discovery quality (his was 'does this trigger change the response of a following benign GET?'), (2) split inspiration sources into 1-3 sentence micro-fragments so the model does not over-anchor, (3) execute each pipeline step in a fresh context with only evidence + scripts passed forward to block bad-reasoning contamination, (4) implement code-validation gates that the LLM cannot rewrite (LLM proposes fingerprint, code verifies it), (5) reserve the human for the cascade step (analyzing a finding for generalizable attack class), not for per-verdict review.

entries.prior_art: Prior 'AI finds bugs' work (XBOW, buttercup DARPA AIxCC, Google's Big Sleep) established that agents can find known-class bugs. The HTTP Terminator's delta is (a) proving AI-proposed novel attack classes (Shared-Parser Confusion, dangling-byte) validated at scale, (b) the AI-vs-Code-vs-Human framing as design axis, and (c) shipping an open-source, reproducible research factory. Closest published methodology is Kettle's own HTTP/1.1 Must Die paper (manual) and Orange Tsai's Confusion Attacks on Apache (partial overlap with Shared-Parser Confusion but Apache-specific).
entries.threat: Any web infrastructure that (a) still terminates upstream HTTP/1.1 and (b) shares parser code between request and response paths is now exposed to a class of attacks that autonomous research pipelines can rediscover at bug-bounty scale in a single overnight run. Specific mechanisms proven live: multipart/byteranges CL.0 desync (200+ sites incl. American bank), dual-matching Content-Length (Meta, SSO servers), CONNECT-tunnel desync (BeyondTrust Secure Remote Access), CVE-2026-63078 (Apache Traffic Server).
entries.conditions: Upstream front-end→back-end connection uses HTTP/1.1. Front-end and back-end disagree on any of: method allow-list, header parsing, body-length semantics, request/response parser separation. Bug-bounty program open at scale (this is what makes the offense easier than the defense).
entries.mitigations: Never terminate upstream HTTP/1.1 — use HTTP/2 or higher end-to-end. Enforce an HTTP method allow-list on both front-end and back-end. Enforce a separate allow-list of methods permitted to carry a request body (POST and possibly PUT/PATCH only; never GET/HEAD/OPTIONS). Do not share parser code between request and response paths.

entries.title: CSS the bomb: sanitized webmail CSS steals tokens, keylogs Outlook, and turns Atlas AI browser into an exfil bot
entries.summary: Gareth Heyes chains allowed HTML/CSS features across Fastmail, Outlook, AOL/Yahoo/Gmail/ProtonMail and OpenAI's Atlas AI browser to defeat webmail CSS sanitization. Techniques include HTML labels that trigger arbitrary UI actions, invisible :before/:after content that feeds one story to the human and another to an AI browser (indirect prompt injection), attribute-selector nesting to brute-force login tokens after a paste-into-draft, CSS hotwiring to hijack any click, and a real-time keylogger via select+opacity plus Chrome interest invokers.
entries.takeaway: CSS sanitizers built as feature allow-lists are not a trust boundary; the only durable defense is strict iframe sandboxing plus killing dangerous selectors, select, and free-form image URLs.

lessons.point: Invisible :before/:after content lets an attacker present two different messages to the human and to an AI browser reading the same email, enabling indirect prompt injection through webmail.
lessons.excerpt: you could use the `:before` and `:after` pseudo-elements to hide the text from the LLM and you could use opacity to hide it from the victim. This creates a disparity between what the victim sees and what the LLM sees, potentially altering the email's context.

lessons.point: CSS attribute selectors, combined with nesting, can brute-force secret URL parameters (e.g. Medium's 12-char login token) inside a webmail draft after a single paste, without JavaScript.
lessons.excerpt: using nesting we can match the start with one selector that's outputted only once and then nest the other selectors to brute-force the token with a smaller amount of CSS

lessons.point: The only defense that actually holds is strict iframe sandboxing plus removing dangerous selectors and select elements; feature-level CSS/HTML allow lists get bypassed by gadgets and mutation.
lessons.excerpt: One of the best methods to protect against these attacks is strict isolation. If you isolate the email message using sandboxed iframes you restrict the ability to break out of trusted boundaries.

lessons.point: CSS hotwiring lets an attacker with allow-listed CSS force the victim's next click, anywhere on the page, to fire a chosen UI action, including multi-step ones.
lessons.excerpt: CSS hotwiring is a technique that allows you to force the victim to click a specific UI action when clicking anywhere on the page **including multi-step actions** using just CSS.

actionable.title: Threat-model webmail-style renderers as adversarial input surfaces for both humans and AI browsers
actionable.detail: For any product rendering third-party HTML/CSS to a user (webmail, comment systems, agent-visible pages): isolate in a sandboxed iframe; strip select and any dangerous selectors (:has, :checked, :focus, :not); route images through a proxy; reject data: URLs; and assume attackers will use :before/:after to differ human vs LLM view. Add a regression test that renders a corpus of PortSwigger's published payloads and confirms none reach the DOM.

entries.prior_art: Apple ANSI-DNS-exfil chain (embracethered) covers CLI-side prompt-injection exfil; CSS-side webmail attacks trace back to Heiderich's mutation XSS and Gerste's font-based CSS exfil. The AI-browser-via-CSS-hidden-content angle is materially new relative to the pool.
entries.threat: A single crafted email lets an attacker (a) spoof or hijack UI actions in Outlook/Fastmail via HTML labels + CSS hotwiring, (b) exfiltrate login tokens and passwords from third-party sites the victim pastes into a webmail draft, (c) inject instructions that only the AI browser sees, causing an AI email assistant to open attacker-controlled tabs and leak the victim's name, and (d) keylog Outlook via CSS/select gadgets. All from allow-listed HTML/CSS with no JavaScript.
entries.conditions: Webmail client renders untrusted HTML/CSS in the same DOM as the trusted UI (no sandboxed iframe isolation), or the user pastes clipboard HTML into a contenteditable draft on Firefox, or an AI browser (e.g. Atlas) processes the email body as prompt context.
entries.mitigations: Sandbox untrusted email content in an iframe with a strict CSP that blocks external image requests and data: URLs. Strip select, dangerous selectors (:has, :checked, :focus, :not), and image URLs pointing to attacker-controllable domains. When an image proxy is available, force all image requests through it. In AI-browser layers, treat CSS-hidden or opacity-zero content as untrusted content the model should not act on.

entries.title: macOS ClickFix campaign moves from open lures to server-side browser-fingerprinting gates that cloak the payload from crawlers
entries.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence documented the same macOS ClickFix infrastructure shifting from serving lures openly in HTML to fronting them with a JavaScript browser-fingerprinting gate. Only visitors whose environment (WebGL GPU signals, toString-counter tripwire, MP4 canPlayType prototype-tamper probe, timezone, touch support) matches a genuine macOS desktop browser see the ClickFix lure; crawlers get blank pages or unrelated decoys.
entries.takeaway: 'Apparently benign' scan results from suspicious domains are unreliable — cloaked infrastructure now decides per-request whether to serve payload, decoy, or blank, so passive analysis systematically underreports these campaigns.

lessons.point: Static/passive scanners systematically miss this campaign because payload is withheld until fingerprint submission — a domain can look benign or blank from a scanner and still be actively serving ClickFix to real macOS users.
lessons.excerpt: Because this decision is made server-side on a per-request basis, a given scan or visit may receive benign or decoy content and still be interacting with malicious infrastructure, so an apparently benign or look-alike response does not mean the domain is safe.

lessons.point: The fingerprinting gate uses WebGL-derived GPU signals as a hardware-authenticity check that distinguishes real Apple silicon from virtualized/emulated/sandbox environments.
lessons.excerpt: One notable check uses WebGL, a browser graphics API normally used to render 2D and 3D content, to retrieve graphics-processing details from the visitor's device. In this campaign, those WebGL-derived GPU signals help distinguish real Apple hardware from virtualized, emulated, software-rendered, or sandboxed environments before the server decides whether to return the ClickFix lure.

lessons.point: Two novel anti-analysis tripwires: (a) a toString() counter that increments if DevTools or a headless log-capture serializes console output; (b) a canPlayType('video/mp4') probe repurposed via a hooked Array.prototype.includes tripwire to detect JS-faked codec support.
lessons.excerpt: The script creates a temporary function whose toString() method increases a counter, then writes that function to the console. In a normal browser, this counter usually remains unchanged. However, if the developer console is open, or if a headless or log-capturing tool serializes console output, the function may be converted to a string, causing the counter to increase.

lessons.point: ClickFix as a delivery mechanism bypasses macOS's application-trust path (quarantine, code signing, notarization) because execution starts from a user-typed Terminal command rather than a downloaded .app bundle.
lessons.excerpt: Because execution starts from a user-run Terminal command rather than a downloaded app bundle, the flow can avoid parts of the normal macOS application trust path, including quarantine handling, code-signing evaluation, and notarization checks typically applied to downloaded applications.

entries.threat: macOS infostealer (MacSync, Atomic Stealer) delivered via ClickFix social engineering, with server-side browser fingerprinting gating who sees the lure.
entries.conditions: User visits a look-alike domain in the campaign's cluster (250+ dictionary-style names containing 'file' token); browser fingerprint indicates genuine macOS + expected geography/browser + no automation instrumentation; user copies Terminal command from a fake 'Verified Publisher' page.
entries.mitigations: Do not rely on 'benign scan' verdicts for suspicious domains — dynamic analysis with authentic-looking fingerprints is required; hunt using domain naming pivots (dictionary-style with 'file' token) plus fingerprint-response combinations; harden Terminal-command copy-paste flows with user education and copy-hook detection.
entries.prior_art: Follow-up to Microsoft's May 2026 ClickFix documentation. Novelty is the server-side fingerprinting gate and its detection-evasion probes — not the ClickFix technique itself.

actionable.title: Assume 'apparently benign' from a passive scanner is unreliable for cloaked infrastructure
actionable.detail: When triaging a suspicious domain, require dynamic evaluation from an authentic-looking fingerprint (real UA, WebGL GPU, timezone, plausible geo). A blank/decoy response is not evidence of safety.
