entries.title: etcd: a READ grant on one key reads everything after it, because the Watch API skipped the range authorization Range/Get applies
entries.summary: A user with READ on a single exact etcd key could call Watch with an open-ended range (clientv3.WithFromKey()) and receive events for every key at or after it. Range/Get and DeleteRange are explicitly unaffected, so this is authorization enforced per API surface rather than centrally - with the streaming endpoint as the one that drifted. Patched in etcd 3.7.1 / 3.6.14 / 3.5.33; reported in part by Anthropic.

lessons.point: The exploitation primitive is IDOR with a range operator: instead of guessing identifiers you widen the bound. Any API that accepts a range, prefix or wildcard needs the authorization check applied to the requested range, not to the caller's grant in isolation.
lessons.excerpt: can use the Watch gRPC API with `clientv3.WithFromKey()` (an open-ended, "from this key to the end of the keyspace" watch) to receive watch events for every key

lessons.point: Subscription endpoints are where per-endpoint authorization drifts - the same pattern as GraphQL subscriptions missing query-level field authz, or Kubernetes treating watch as a verb distinct from get/list. The advisory gives no root cause, so that reading is our inference; what it does state is which surfaces are unaffected.
lessons.excerpt: This is an authorization bypass in etcd's RBAC enforcement for the Watch API; Range/Get and DeleteRange requests are not affected.

lessons.point: Until patched, the correct mental model for a grant audit is that partial READ is not partial: hold every READ grant to the standard of full read access from that key onward.
lessons.excerpt: Any READ grant - even on one key - can be leveraged via Watch to read everything after it.

entries.takeaway: If your read endpoint and your stream endpoint enforce authorization in different code, you have two policies and only test one.
entries.threat: A low-privilege authenticated etcd client reads the bulk of the keyspace via Watch.
entries.conditions: Clusters with authentication enabled and meaningfully partitioned READ grants; the advisory gives fixed versions only and no affected-version range.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to the patched releases; audit and tighten READ grants; restrict network reach to the client gRPC port.
entries.prior_art: Known bug class rather than a new one: GraphQL subscription resolvers missing query-level authz, WebSocket/SSE channel joins not re-checking per-topic ACLs, Kafka topic-pattern subscribe vs per-topic ACLs, and Kubernetes RBAC treating watch separately from get/list. Range-widening as an authz bypass is IDOR/BOLA with a range operator.
entries.verify_note: Verifier scored novelty 20/100 - the 'stream endpoint skips the read endpoint's authz check' pattern has many documented prior instances, so only the instance is new. It also flagged that the advisory gives no root cause (the per-endpoint-drift explanation is our inference and is labelled as such), that 'only Watch' overstates a list of three unaffected request types, and that Watch delivers events rather than a keyspace snapshot. Held for review as a known class.

entries.title: What Is AI Pentesting and How Does It Work?
entries.summary: Snyk lays out a four-part reference architecture for AI pentesting: a reasoning model that plans reconnaissance/hypothesis/probing/exploitation/chaining, deterministic tools for exhaustive-payload work (a DAST engine, not the LLM enumerating payloads token-by-token), an independent validator model that confirms exploitability before a finding is reported, and prior context about what other tools already found so expensive reasoning is spent on the flaws that require it. The category exists to cover context-dependent flaws (BOLA/IDOR, cross-tenant leakage, auth bypass, chained business-logic exploits) that no signature can reach. Two hard reliability numbers: on autonomous red-teaming benchmarks the strongest model solves 61% overall but under 26% on harder system-exploitation tasks, and raw AI tooling has been observed to hallucinate findings around 30% of the time — which is the empirical case for a separate validator model.
entries.takeaway: AI pentesting is a four-part orchestrated system — reasoning model, deterministic tools, independent validator, prior context — and the failure mode of skipping any one of those is either hallucinated findings, redundant scanner work, or a validator conflict of interest.

lessons.point: AI pentesting is defined as an orchestrated four-part system, not a lone LLM — reasoning model plans, deterministic DAST engine handles known-class exhaustive testing, a separate validator model confirms exploitability, and prior scanner context focuses reasoning at flaws that require it.
lessons.excerpt: A modern AI pentester is not a single model pointed at a URL. It's an orchestrated system with four parts: A reasoning model that plans the assessment: reconnaissance, hypothesis, probing, exploitation, and chaining, the way a human tester approaches an engagement. Deterministic tools in which the model calls for the well-understood work. Exhaustive payload testing of known vulnerability classes is faster and cheaper handled by a dynamic testing (DAST) engine than by a model enumerating payloads token by token. An independent validator, which is a separate model or engine, confirms that a finding is genuinely exploitable before it is reported.

lessons.point: The raw AI-pentest reliability floor is roughly 30% hallucinated findings; the empirical justification for a separate validator is the false-positive rate you inherit if you skip it.
lessons.excerpt: Raw AI tooling has been observed to hallucinate findings roughly 30% of the time, and a false positive you can't trust is worse than no finding. Credible systems put an independent validator between the model and the report.

lessons.point: Autonomous red-team benchmark reality check: the strongest model solves 61% of challenges overall but falls below 26% on harder system-exploitation tasks — which sets the ceiling on any 'lone frontier model as pentester' pitch.
lessons.excerpt: On one autonomous red-teaming benchmark, the strongest model solved 61% of challenges overall but fell below 26% on harder system-exploitation tasks.

lessons.point: The class of vulnerabilities AI pentesting exists to cover is context-dependent flaws — BOLA/IDOR, cross-tenant data leakage, auth bypass, privilege escalation, chained business-logic exploits — which by definition have no signature and cannot be detected by pattern-matching tools.
lessons.excerpt: Context-dependent vulnerabilities have no signature. You cannot write a rule for "user A shouldn't be able to read user B's invoice," because it depends on the application's intended behavior. This class includes broken object-level authorization (BOLA/IDOR), cross-tenant data leakage, authentication bypasses, privilege escalation, and chained business-logic exploits.

lessons.point: Six evaluation criteria for vendor claims: independent validation, prior-scanner context, continuous re-test, verifiable proof-of-concept output, low FP rate, complementary to (not replacement of) human testing — usable as a scorecard when comparing offerings.
lessons.excerpt: A useful criterion when comparing tools is asking these 6 questions: Independent validation — does a separate step confirm exploitability, or does the finding model grade itself? Context — does it know what your existing scanners already found, so it hunts flaws instead of re-finding bugs? Continuous — does it re-test on every change, or is it another point-in-time snapshot? Verifiable output — runnable proof of concept plus a reasoning trace you can audit? Low false positives — will your team trust the findings enough to act? Complementary — does it extend your scanners and human testing, rather than claiming to replace them?

actionable.title: AI-pentesting evaluation scorecard: hold every vendor to the four-part architecture and the six-question criterion
actionable.detail: When comparing autonomous / AI-pentesting offerings, require public disclosure on: (1) which model plans, which model validates, and whether they are the same model — same-model self-grading fails the independence test, (2) how the DAST engine and prior-scan context are wired in, (3) the false-positive rate on a fixed corpus (Snyk's public number for their deterministic engine is 0.08%), (4) reproducibility of findings across identical runs, (5) the runnable PoC and reasoning trace attached to each finding, and (6) evidence the tool is complementary rather than a replacement claim. Also enforce production-safety governance: scope enforcement, an independent validation step, reproducibility, and audit trails — the article's stated position is that these controls are harder to build than the offensive capability itself.

entries.prior_art: The 'AI-augmented pentesting' category has been building through 2026 with XBOW, ProjectDiscovery, Anthropic's vulnerability-discovery program, and PortSwigger's HTTP Terminator. Snyk's delta here is a concrete four-part reference architecture (reasoning / DAST / validator / prior context), quantitative floors on raw-LLM reliability (~30% hallucinated findings, 61%/26% autonomous-red-team benchmark split), and a six-question buyer scorecard. Related to the same-week 'generator can't be validator' Snyk post — same thesis, pentesting-specific framing.
entries.threat: Any team deploying AI pentesting as a raw LLM pointed at a URL (rather than as an orchestrated system with a separate validator): expected outcome is ~30% hallucinated findings and coverage that collapses on harder system-exploitation classes (sub-26% on the cited benchmark), which means an unusable false-positive rate and a false sense of coverage on the exact class the tool is bought to catch.
entries.conditions: Same model plans and grades its own findings (no independent validator). No deterministic DAST layer for exhaustive known-class payload testing. No prior-scanner context; the model re-discovers cataloged bugs at high token cost. Findings ship without a runnable PoC and reasoning trace.
entries.mitigations: Independent validator model or engine between finding and report; validator is not the reasoning model. DAST engine carries payload enumeration for known-class flaws; LLM does not enumerate token-by-token. Feed the pipeline prior-scanner findings so reasoning is spent on flaws that require it. Every reported finding ships a runnable PoC and full reasoning trace for human audit. Production governance: scope enforcement, reproducibility, audit trails as a precondition for running against live systems.

entries.title: Introducing Semgrep Agentic Workflows: Automate Deep Vulnerability Hunting at Scale
entries.summary: Semgrep is shipping nine pre-built Agentic Workflows in public beta that pair frontier reasoning (Claude Opus) with the Semgrep Pro Engine and a code-slicer named Mandoline to hunt authentication, injection, and business-logic flaws across 70+ CWEs. The architectural claim worth extracting is not the launch itself but the empirical delta: their AI+program-analysis combination finds 3.5x more true positives than Opus 4.8 alone at 19% lower cost per true positive. The design principle is that the model is fed exactly the sliced context it needs, deterministic analysis carries taint tracing and inter-file work, and the LLM only reasons about exploitability — an explicit AI-vs-code role split.
entries.takeaway: The AI-augmented SAST win is not "replace static analysis with an LLM" — it is "feed the LLM sliced context and let deterministic taint tracing carry the correctness-critical steps."

lessons.point: The measurable AI+SAST result is a 3.5x true-positive uplift over the frontier model alone, at 19% lower cost per true positive — concrete numbers to hold vendor claims to when evaluating "agentic" SAST offerings.
lessons.excerpt: In our own benchmarking, that combination finds 3.5x more true positives than Opus 4.8 running alone, at 19% lower cost per true positive.

lessons.point: The transferable architecture is program-analysis + code-slicer (Mandoline) + frontier model for reasoning — the deterministic layer carries taint tracing and inter-file analysis, and the model only reasons about exploitability on a curated context window.
lessons.excerpt: Each Agentic Workflow draws on the same toolkit: the Semgrep Pro Engine and Pro rules for deterministic analysis such as taint tracing and interfile analysis, Semgrep Mandoline (a code slicer internal to Agentic Workflows built specifically for handing agents exactly the context and code they need), and frontier AI models such as Claude Opus for reasoning about exploitability.

lessons.point: The threat driver is symmetric capability uplift: attackers now have on-demand pentester-grade reasoning at attacker cadence, and traditional pre-AI tools plus human review cannot keep pace — defender AppSec has to match the reasoning layer, not just improve rule coverage.
lessons.excerpt: AppSec teams can’t outrun these attackers using traditional pre-AI tools, nor by relying on humans reviewing all of the code being generated. To give AppSec teams a step up in defensive capabilities, today we’re launching nine Agentic Workflows that find the subtle authentication, injection, and business logic flaws that matter most.

actionable.title: Evaluate AI-augmented SAST on the 3.5x-TPs-at-lower-cost benchmark, not on flat CWE-coverage tables
actionable.detail: When comparing agentic AppSec tools, hold vendors to two questions: (1) what is the true-positive uplift over the frontier model running solo on the same corpus, and (2) what is the cost per true positive at that uplift? Semgrep's public number is 3.5x TPs at 19% lower cost/TP using program-analysis + code-slicer + Claude Opus. Anything below that ratio is a claim that the vendor's slicing/inter-file analysis is doing less work than a raw model prompt — which means the money is going to token cost, not to reduction in reviewer triage. Also require the vendor to disclose the slicer or context-selection layer, because that is where the correctness-critical work happens.

entries.prior_art: Prior claims in the pool around AI-augmented static analysis (Snyk DeepCode, GitHub Copilot autofix, autonomous research pipelines like PortSwigger's HTTP Terminator) already established the 'LLM + deterministic engine' architecture. The delta here is a specific quantitative uplift (3.5x TPs / 19% lower cost per TP) and public identification of a code-slicer (Mandoline) as the load-bearing component alongside taint tracing.
entries.threat: Enterprises deploying naked-LLM SAST (a raw model reading whole repos) pay high token cost and get lower true-positive rates than an equivalent pipeline that combines deterministic taint tracing and inter-file analysis with an LLM reasoning step on a sliced context window — which means naked-LLM SAST is dominated on both cost and quality.
entries.conditions: The workload is scanning application code for authentication / injection / business-logic flaws. Reviewer capacity is finite and false-positive rate directly determines whether findings get triaged. The organization has budget for either a program-analysis layer plus a frontier model, or a frontier model alone.
entries.mitigations: Prefer AI+program-analysis pipelines over frontier-model-only scanners for CWE-in-code work. Require vendors to publish TP-uplift-vs-solo-model and cost-per-TP numbers on a fixed corpus. Insist on visibility into the code-slicing / context-selection layer so it can be audited. Keep human triage in the loop for the highest-severity findings; use the pipeline to filter, not to auto-close.

entries.title: Why AI-assisted attacks made software supply chain security its own category
entries.summary: Vendor essay from Chainguard framing software supply chain security as its own Gartner category, pegged to the June 2026 Magic Quadrant. Core argument: AI compresses the vulnerability-to-exploitation window on both sides, and agent skill registries are a new supply-chain artifact — cites a February 2026 finding of hundreds of malicious agent skills. Positions Chainguard's build-from-source approach as the prevention alternative to scan-and-detect.
entries.takeaway: Agent skills are a new supply-chain artifact class alongside containers, libraries, and CI/CD workflows — treat them the same way you already treat npm packages (provenance, review gates, minimal trust), not as configuration.

lessons.point: Agent skills have become a supply-chain surface: attackers publish malicious skills that direct agents to install credential-harvesting malware.
lessons.excerpt: Consider agent skills. In February 2026, researchers found hundreds of malicious skills in community registries, quietly directing AI agents to install credential-harvesting malware. The instruction set that makes an agent more capable became a new hiding place for an attack. It's the same software supply chain story, but with a new artifact.

lessons.point: AI compresses the vulnerability-to-exploitation window on both sides, so 'detect after ingest' security postures lose the race by construction.
lessons.excerpt: The window between "a vulnerability exists" and "a vulnerability is being exploited" is collapsing, and waiting to detect an attack after it launches means reacting inside a window that keeps getting shorter.

lessons.point: The rate at which agents pull in dependencies makes 'we'll check it later' review policies untenable.
lessons.excerpt: Open source makes up over 90 percent of the code most organizations ship, and AI accelerates how much of it you pull in. Agents install dependencies, wire up CI/CD workflows, and adopt new components with very little human review.

actionable.title: Add agent skills to your supply-chain inventory alongside containers and packages
actionable.detail: Extend existing supply-chain controls (provenance attestation, allowlists, review gates) to agent skills consumed from community registries. Do not classify skills as configuration; they carry executable instructions that steer tool-enabled agents.

entries.prior_art: Standard supply-chain security literature (SLSA, sigstore, provenance attestation). The 'malicious agent skills' finding was reported earlier in 2026 by third-party researchers and covered widely; this post is a marketing recap tied to the Gartner MQ, not new research.
entries.threat: Agents pulling in dependencies, CI/CD workflows, or agent skills at machine speed adopt malicious artifacts (typosquatted packages, backdoored containers, poisoned skills) before any human review, enabling credential harvesting or code execution in engineer/agent environments.
entries.conditions: Engineering teams delegate dependency selection to coding agents. Agent skill registries used as untrusted-by-default input. No enforced provenance/signature gate on ingested artifacts. Detect-and-remediate posture (post-ingest scanning) rather than admit-only-trusted-artifacts.
entries.mitigations: Prefer signed, provenance-attested artifacts (containers, packages, skills). Constrain agents to a curated allowlist of registries/mirrors. Require automated PR gates for agent-authored dependency changes. Treat agent skills as code, not config: review, version, sign.

entries.title: Shescape shell-injection via unescaped CMD parentheses (GHSA-w4hw-qcx7-56pr) — one of four per-shell bypasses
entries.summary: Shescape, a popular Node.js library whose whole purpose is to safely escape untrusted arguments for a shell, failed to neutralize parentheses on Windows CMD, letting an attacker break out of a conditional and inject commands via the escape/escapeAll APIs (CVSS 9.2, patched in 2.1.14 / 3.0.1). It is one of four Shescape advisories in this batch — alongside Zsh/Dash path-disclosure and quadratic-DoS bugs — showing that per-shell quoting edge cases keep producing bypasses. The recurring lesson: shell-escaping libraries are fragile across shells and OSes because each shell has its own metacharacter grammar, and a single missed construct re-opens injection.

lessons.point: An escaping library missing a single shell metacharacter class (parentheses in CMD) fully re-opens command injection despite doing its job everywhere else.
lessons.excerpt: The escape functions do not neutralize parentheses `(` and `)` in Windows CMD contexts, enabling command injection through conditional statement manipulation.

lessons.point: The bypass exploits CMD-specific syntax (closing a conditional block), so it only triggers when the command already places the escaped value inside a CMD construct — a per-shell, context-dependent edge case.
lessons.excerpt: Payload: "x) else if a==a (echo y"  Command: if defined FALSY (echo ${escapedPayload})  Result: Outputs "y" instead of empty string

lessons.point: The root cause is classed as both OS command injection and improper neutralization of escape/control sequences — i.e. the escaping logic itself is the defect, not caller misuse.
lessons.excerpt: CWE-78: OS Command Injection; CWE-150: Improper neutralization of escape/control sequences

lessons.point: This is one of four concurrent Shescape advisories (CMD injection, Zsh/Dash path disclosure, quadratic DoS), evidencing that shell-escaping is a recurring, cross-shell/cross-OS fragility rather than a one-off bug.
lessons.excerpt: This impacts users of Shescape on Windows that explicitly configure `shell` to CMD, or `true` with the default shell being CMD, using the `escape` and `escapeAll` APIs.

entries.takeaway: Escaping untrusted input for a shell is a leaky abstraction — prefer passing arguments as an argv array to a shell-less exec over trusting any escape library, because each shell keeps yielding new metacharacter bypasses.
entries.prior_art: The broader 'incomplete neutralization yields command injection' class (CWE-78/CWE-150) and Shescape's own prior per-shell escaping advisories; the analyst's cited Kemp LoadMaster null-byte-gap-to-RCE is the nearest thematic match.
entries.threat: An attacker who controls a command argument passed through Shescape's escape/escapeAll on Windows CMD can break out of the intended command context (e.g. a conditional block) and execute arbitrary commands (CVSS 9.2).
entries.conditions: Runtime is Windows with the shell resolved to CMD (explicit shell=CMD, or shell=true with CMD as default); Application uses Shescape escape or escapeAll APIs (v2.x < 2.1.14 or v3.x < 3.0.1); The escaped value is interpolated into a command where parentheses are syntactically meaningful (e.g. an if/for block)
entries.mitigations: Upgrade Shescape to 2.1.14 or 3.0.1+; Prefer argv-array exec (execFile/spawn without shell) over any string-escaping approach; Temporary workaround: strip or reject '(' and ')' in untrusted input before escaping; Plan v2->v3 migration before v2 EOL (2026-09-28)
entries.verify_note: GHSA page confirms CVSS 9.2, CWE-78/150, the exact PoC payload and CMD conditional, and escape/escapeAll scope; a fresh concrete CVE instance of a well-known escaping-fragility class, so useful but low-novelty.

entries.title: Introducing Internal Network Scanning: see your network the way an attacker inside it would
entries.summary: ProjectDiscovery released an unauthenticated internal-network scanner that runs Nuclei templates from inside a segment rather than banner-matching against CVE lists. The framing is that as AI has driven annual CVE volume toward 50,000 and the mean time-to-exploit has inverted to negative 7 days, coverage-first internal scanning produces a backlog you can never clear in time; a scanner that ships only confirmed, request/response-proven exposures from where an attacker would land is the more useful primitive. Runs alongside credentialed scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) which cover patch-level on managed hosts; the pd-agent covers reachability of everything routable, including the forgotten server and Kubernetes pod/service CIDRs that credentialed tools miss.
entries.takeaway: In the AI-bent-curve era, internal scanning that returns 'potentially vulnerable' banner matches is a queue, not a control; wire a Nuclei-style unauthenticated agent in every segment so what you fix is what an intruder could actually trigger from that beachhead.

lessons.point: The vulnerability curve has inverted: MTT-exploit for prioritized CVEs is now negative — exploitation begins before a patch exists — so coverage-first scanning backlogs are structurally too slow.
lessons.excerpt: annual CVE volume has climbed toward 50,000 and for the vulnerabilities attackers actually prioritize, the mean time to exploit has inverted from roughly 63 days to negative 7 days meaning exploitation often begins before a patch exists.

lessons.point: Credentialed scanners answer 'is it patched'; they don't answer 'is it reachable from where an attacker lands' — the internal segment where the pivot lives is exactly the coverage gap.
lessons.excerpt: Credentialed scanning is the most reliable way to know what's installed and unpatched across the hosts you manage and nothing here replaces it. What it doesn't tell you is whether the service is reachable and the path exploitable from where an attacker actually lands, and its coverage ends at the hosts you hold credentials or an agent for, which is rarely the forgotten server or the unmanaged device.

lessons.point: Segmentation without inside-the-segment scanning is a paper control: an agent that already reached the segment walks the same routable paths the pd-agent enumerates.
lessons.excerpt: Segmentation slows lateral movement but doesn't stop it once the pivot host is already inside the segment, which is as true on a corporate network as it was there.

actionable.title: Deploy an unauthenticated Nuclei-class agent per segment and treat its confirmed findings as the patch queue
actionable.detail: Install pd-agent (or an equivalent Nuclei-driven internal scanner) in every distinct trust segment — production, staging, per-region, per-acquisition, per-office. Scope discovery by where the agent sits (host subnets + Kubernetes pod/service CIDRs) so each finding is attributable to a segment owner. Stop triaging banner-match output; escalate only what returned a proof-of-exploit request/response. Keep credentialed scanning (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) for patch-level accuracy on managed hosts — the two lists cover different questions and should be run in parallel, not as substitutes.

entries.prior_art: Nuclei/httpx have been publicly usable as internal scanners for years; the packaged pd-agent + platform + per-segment reachability model is the delta. The 'MTT-exploit is now negative' framing echoes VulnCheck's Known Exploited list observations and Google Project Zero's shrinking-window data.
entries.threat: Defensive teams whose only internal-scanning control is a credentialed patch scanner report zero coverage on the forgotten intranet WordPress, unmanaged network device, or spun-up Kubernetes dashboard that an inside attacker reaches first — so post-phish lateral movement to the domain controller / vCenter / backups goes unmapped in scan output.
entries.conditions: Internal scanning is limited to credentialed patch scans on managed hosts. No unauthenticated reachability check runs from inside the segment where an attacker would land. Kubernetes pod/service CIDRs and shadow-owned assets are not in the scan scope.
entries.mitigations: Run an unauthenticated Nuclei-driven agent from inside every distinct network segment. Keep credentialed scanners for patch-level truth on managed hosts (complementary, not redundant). Include Kubernetes pod/service CIDRs and acquisition/office networks in discovery scope. Treat only findings with a captured request/response proof as urgent — not banner matches.

entries.title: Cryptographic advisories are dominated by skipped code checks, not broken math — a range check would have stopped a 9.8 ECDSA bypass
entries.summary: Semgrep's Diptendu Kar analyzed the full GHSA advisory set filed under OWASP A04:2025 (Cryptographic Failures) and found the top CWEs are improper signature verification (CWE-347) and use of a broken/risky algorithm (CWE-327) — both of which are code-level omissions, not primitive breaks. Walkthrough example: CVE-2021-43572, a real FinTech signing library rated 9.8, was defeated by sending r=0, s=0 because the code never enforced 1 <= r,s <= n-1. Fix is a four-line range check.
entries.takeaway: Most 'crypto' bugs in the wild aren't crypto — they're validation checks that never run in the wrapper code around the primitive. Reviewers don't need a math background; they need to attack the input path.

lessons.point: At scale, cryptographic advisories cluster on skipped checks rather than broken primitives.
lessons.excerpt: over and over, the math was intact and the code had simply skipped a check

lessons.point: The top-ranked CWEs under OWASP A04 are validation problems, which the author explicitly reframes as code bugs.
lessons.excerpt: Improper signature verification and algorithm confusion are _code_ problems. A validation check that doesn't run can allow untrusted input.

lessons.point: A real 9.8 ECDSA bug (CVE-2021-43572) is defeated by the laziest possible attacker input; you don't need to touch the math to find it.
lessons.excerpt: The answer is zero. Send `r=0` and `s=0` then the whole computation collapses to zero on both sides. The signature validates since `0==0`.

lessons.point: The advisories recur across languages and libraries because reviewers keep deferring to 'the crypto library will handle it.'
lessons.excerpt: The wrapper that checks input, compares two values, or picks which algorithm to use sails through reviews because everybody assumes it is over their head.

actionable.title: Add a 'boring-crypto-check' pass to code review checklists
actionable.detail: When reviewing code that calls a crypto verify() function, enumerate what an attacker controls on both sides of the final comparison, and confirm each attacker-controlled input passes an explicit range/type check before the primitive runs. Do the same for algorithm selection: is the alg field attacker-controlled, and if so is 'none' or a weakened alg reachable? This is a reviewer skill, not a cryptographer skill.

entries.prior_art: Classic JWT alg=none, invalid-curve attacks, and Wycheproof-style test suites make the same point; this piece is a fresh restatement grounded in the current GHSA distribution.
entries.threat: Attackers submit malformed but well-formed-looking cryptographic payloads (all-zero ECDSA sigs, wrong-curve points, alg=none JWTs) to endpoints that call a crypto library's verify() but omit input validation. Result: signature-verified user impersonation, integrity bypass, or algorithm downgrade — CVSS 9.x-class bugs from a four-line omission.
entries.conditions: Application performs cryptographic signature verification or algorithm selection with attacker-controlled inputs, and the wrapper code around the primitive does not enforce 1 <= r,s <= n-1 (for ECDSA) or reject attacker-influenced algorithm identifiers before dispatching to the library.
entries.mitigations: Add explicit range checks on all numeric signature components before calling verify. Reject algorithm identifiers not on a static allowlist. Prefer AEAD/high-level constructs over hand-assembled signature verification. Add SAST rules (Semgrep-style) that flag verify() call sites lacking pre-condition checks.
